summary: SoilSense is a decision-support web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect soil health and adapt to a changing climate. Using NASA POWER climate data, it compares a farmer’s current rotation with two suggested alternatives, scored on soil health, water, climate fit, and income and weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. Each option comes with plain-language reasons, Low/Medium/High risk meters, and data gaps, and a worst-year replay tests every rotation against the driest year on record. A multilingual assistant (English, Arabic, and Bengali) answers questions by text or voice, a weather panel gives short-term alerts, and a downloadable report tells the farmer what to do. SoilSense supports, and does not replace, farmer and local expert judgment.
details:
What it does and how it works

SoilSense is a web app that helps farmers compare crop rotations that protect soil health and adapt to a changing climate. The farmer chooses their current three-crop rotation, their available irrigation water, and how much they value saving water, soil health, and income.

It does the following:

  1. Loads NASA POWER daily climate data (2001-2025) for the region and calculates typical rainfall, rainfall and temperature trends, and the driest year on record, using robust statistics so extreme years don’t distort the results.
  2. Detects and corrects suspect data. Our rainfall record contained an implausible episode in August 2024, with up to 514 mm in a single day, while the next-highest day in the other 24 years is about 152 mm. SoilSense replaces such days with typical values for those dates, keeps the original values, and shows a data-quality notice in the app.
  3. Generates all valid multi-year rotations, filtering out any where a crop family follows itself, since that spreads pests and disease.
  4. Scores each rotation on soil health (legumes adding nitrogen before demanding crops, deep roots), water supply against crop need, heat and drought tolerance, and income, weighted by the farmer’s priorities.
  5. Shows the farmer’s current rotation next to two suggested alternatives, each with plain-language reasons, Low/Medium/High risk meters, and a note of data gaps and what needs local verification.
  6. Runs a worst-year replay, re-scoring every option under the driest year on record to show which rotation holds up best.
  7. Produces a plain-text farmer report (recommended action, reasons, comparison, dry-year outlook, water and soil actions, and gaps) that can be read in the app and downloaded.
  8. Includes a multilingual AI assistant (Arabic, English, and Bengali) that answers farmers’ questions using the tool’s own calculated results. Farmers can type or speak their questions and have the answers read aloud.
  9. Shows a short-term weather panel with severity levels and alerts, using forecast data from Open-Meteo.
  10. Includes an irrigation and watering panel that helps farmers plan water use.
  11. Lets farmers upload a photo of a plant for analysis by a vision model. It gives an early hint, never a diagnosis, never suggests pesticide or chemical doses, and tells the farmer when to call a local extension officer.

Benefits and intended impact

SoilSense turns long-term satellite data into clear choices for farmers with no technical background. It helps them see how their current practice compares with alternatives, protect soil, use scarce water more carefully, and test plans against a bad year before committing. Plain language, three languages, and voice make it usable for farmers with limited technical or reading experience. It is built to support farmers and local agricultural experts, not replace their judgment.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA POWER (temperature, rainfall, solar radiation); Open-Meteo (weather forecast and air quality)
  • Language and libraries: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow
  • Interface: Streamlit
  • AI assistant: language models (Gemini, Groq, or OpenRouter free tiers) with tool calling, vision models for plant photos, and a rule-based fallback mode that needs no key
  • Voice: browser text-to-speech for read-aloud answers, and Whisper (through Groq) for voice questions
  • Collaboration: GitHub

What is creative about it

  • It compares whole multi-year rotations, including the farmer’s own, instead of forecasting a single season.
  • Worst-year replay lets farmers stress-test each plan against a real past extreme.
  • It handles messy satellite data honestly: it detects a suspect rainfall episode, corrects it, and shows the correction.
  • Every recommendation is explainable: reasons, risks, and data gaps are always shown.
  • Recommendations are personalized by the farmer’s priorities.
  • A multilingual assistant explains results in Arabic, English, and Bengali, by text or voice, and is built on the tool’s own numbers, not on guesses.
  • It refuses to give pesticide or chemical doses and refers farmers to their local agricultural extension office.
  • It goes beyond rotation planning to give farmers daily tools: weather alerts, irrigation planning, plant photo hints, and a downloadable report, all in their own language.

Factors our team considered

  • Uncertainty: rainfall in arid regions varies a lot, and our data contained one extreme year (2024) that would have distorted averages, so we used median and robust trend methods and corrected and flagged the unusual days.
  • Satellite vs. ground data: NASA POWER values are satellite and model estimates, not rain gauge readings, so results should be verified locally. The 2024 correction is a rule-based judgment and should be checked against ground observations.
  • Transparency: we chose clear, rule-based scoring over a black-box model so farmers can see why each option was suggested.
  • Limits: crop values are simplified estimates, and the current version covers one region.
  • Language access: many farmers in the region work in Arabic or Bengali, so the assistant supports those languages.
  • Location limits: the rotation scores come from one site’s climate file, so for farms far from it the assistant warns that results need expert review.
  • Accessibility: plain language, voice input, and read-aloud answers for farmers with limited technical experience.
  • Safety: photo results are early hints, not diagnoses, and the app never gives pesticide or chemical doses.
  • Forecasts: weather alerts are model forecasts, not official warnings, and say so.
  • Future work: more NASA datasets (SMAP soil moisture, MODIS vegetation health), more regions, soil analysis, push notifications, and machine learning for trend forecasting.
